rashi:a1.1: Comes with an authorization: the two fathers wrote authorizations, each to the other, and the holder of the authorization comes and claims from him: Whichever way you look at it, if mine died, return mine to me; and if my fellow’s died, return his to me, since I hold his authorization.
rashi:a2.1: Adrakhta: an authorization. [We do not write one] for movable property: since it is not at hand, it looks like a lie. Perhaps he holds nothing of this man’s at all, and the witnesses would be signing a lie.
rashi:a2.2: Where he denied it: [where] the borrower [denied the debt] to the lender, the lender can no longer write an authorization for it, because it looks like a lie.
rashi:a3.1: Rav Huna teaches: concerning two women of two men who had not given birth and who bore, unobserved, two males and a female, the priest has nothing here. And this is so even though one of them is a firstborn whichever way you look at it: if one woman bore the two males, one of them is a firstborn; and if she bore a male and a female, her fellow turns out to have borne a male alone, and he is a firstborn. Even so, the son is not obligated to redeem himself, for he can say to [the priest]: Perhaps I am not the firstborn, but my fellow is.
rashi:a4.1: With one man and two women you do not find it: since there is certainly one firstborn, he gives five sela to the priest. That is why [the tanna] does not teach it, for all the cases in which he taught “the priest has nothing here” are the same whether for one man and his two wives or for two wives of two men.
rashi:a5.1: Mishna. If the son died within thirty: this refers also to ordinary, certain firstborns [not only to the intermingled ones above].
rashi:a5.2: He must return: since it was a nefel [a nonviable birth], and he is not obligated in redemption until after thirty days.
rashi:a5.3: Like the day before it: even though he gave, [the priest] must return it to him.
rashi:a6.1: Gemara. From the wilderness: here it is written: “And those that are to be redeemed, from a month old shall you redeem” (Numbers 18:15–16), and of the wilderness it is written: “Number all the firstborn males … from a month old and upward” (Numbers 3:40).
rashi:a7.1: He is uncertain whether we derive it from there. For since “and upward” was needed in valuations, “And if it be from sixty years old and upward,” and [the Gemara] in tractate Arakhin (18a) derives “year,” “year” by verbal analogy, that just as the sixtieth year is treated like the years below it, as a stringency, so too the fifth year and the twentieth year are treated like those below them, even though that is a leniency, the same applies to “a month old”: the thirtieth day is like the days below it, even though that is a leniency. And [Arakhin] does not derive “month,” “month” from the wilderness, that one would not be valuated until after thirty days.
rashi:a7.2: They are: [the verses] of valuations and of the wilderness of Sinai are two verses that come as one, and they do not teach about the redemption of the son.
rashi:a9.1: Or perhaps, when we say that two verses do not teach, that applies to the world at large, to matters that do not speak of a firstborn or of valuations, as if “month” were written about some other matter.
rashi:a9.2: But for themselves: such as the firstborns of future generations from the firstborns of the wilderness, since both speak of a firstborn, they do teach. And because we are uncertain, he says: If he gave, he does not take it back; and if he did not give, he does not give.
rashi:a10.1: With regard to mourning: if a child dies within thirty [days], mourning does not take effect on his father, for one may say it was a nefel.
rashi:a11.1: Mishna. That he was not redeemed: for people do not usually redeem within thirty [days]; [so he is presumed unredeemed] until he brings proof.
rashi:a11.2: After thirty, the presumption is that he was redeemed: for the priest is the one seeking to take money from another, and his position is weaker.
rashi:a11.3: Until they tell him: [until people tell] the son that his father instructed at the time of his death that he had not been redeemed. And a statement suffices, without full testimony, because this presumption that he was redeemed is not a strong presumption, as most people do not pay their debt right away. And here one cannot say “until he brings proof,” because here the son can say to the priest: My father gave it to some other priest.
rashi:a11.4: For his mitzva is upon his father: the mitzva of redeeming this father was upon his own father, who has died, and the mitzva of his son is upon him.
rashi:a12.1: Gemara. Everyone agrees: if he said to him, “Let my son be redeemed from now,” it is not a redemption but merely a gift, since within thirty [days] redemption does not apply. And if he said within thirty, “Here is the money for you, and after thirty let the redemption of my son take effect,” and the money is still intact in the priest’s hand after thirty, he is certainly redeemed, as if he had given it to him now.
rashi:a13.1: Were squandered: they are no longer intact.
rashi:a13.2: The betrothal of a woman: for if he gives her something now and says to her, “Be betrothed after thirty days,” she is betrothed, as we say in tractate Kiddushin (59a).
rashi:b4.1: Come and hear: from our mishna: If the father died within thirty, the presumption is that he was not redeemed, etc.
rashi:b4.2: We read: “until he brings proof.” And if he brings proof he is redeemed, which is difficult for Shmuel. [The printed Gemara, and the English here, read “until they tell him that he is redeemed.”]
rashi:b8.1: And his own: for his own five sela the priest goes and seizes from liened property, since the priest’s lien came first. That is what [the mishna] says, “for his mitzva is upon his father”: that is, those properties became liened to the priest from his father’s time.
rashi:b8.2: And with these five unencumbered ones he redeems his son: right away. For if he gave the unencumbered ones for his own redemption, his son could no longer be redeemed, since perhaps the buyers’ lien came before his son’s birth.
rashi:b9.1: Is not like one written in a document: so if he gave the unencumbered ones for his son’s redemption, he himself could no longer be redeemed, since the priest cannot seize from the buyers.
rashi:b10.1: Mishna. A Tyrian maneh: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b11.1: Fifty of the rapist and of the seducer: that is, and likewise the fifty of the rapist, etc.
rashi:b11.2: All of them in the shekel of the Sanctuary: which is twenty ma’a, and those ma’a are of the coinage of the Tyrian maneh. The Gemara explains why the tanna needed to go back and teach this, etc.
rashi:b11.3: Except for shekels: the shekels brought to the chamber in Adar; one brings there only coins of half-shekels.
rashi:b12.1: Gemara. The maneh of Tyre: the one current in the province of Tyre, whose sela is four zuz, and the zuz is the weight of a gold coin weighing two and a half pshitin by iron weight.
rashi:b12.2: Rabbi Ami says: the Tyrian sela is the Arabian, Ishmaelite, dinar. [My teacher] did not explain its measure to me, but I found in a responsum of the Babylonian Geonim that seven of the dinars mentioned throughout the Talmud, the dinar being six silver ma’a, make ten of those of Arabia; and in Arabic they call it migra’ot.
rashi:b12.4: Eight of which are sold: eight of them for a dinar.
tosafot:a2.1: In brief: [On “That applies where he denied it.”] Tosafot ask what one can say according to the first version in Merubba (Bava Kamma 70a), which does not distinguish between a respondent who denied and one who did not. They ask the same from Shevuat HaEdut (Shevuot 33b), where the Gemara asks how “a maneh of so-and-so is in so-and-so’s hand” can be claimed by another, answers “where he comes with an authorization,” objects from the Nehardeans, and answers “that applies where he denied it.” That passage can be set in a deposit, even according to the first version: since a deposit can be consecrated (Bava Batra 88a, the man who brought gourds to the river bank), one can also authorize another to claim it, for it is one reason. For our passage they offer several answers: it may speak of land and follow Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], who holds below (51a) that one may redeem with land, and for land an authorization is written; or it follows Rabbi Natan, by whose rule one may take from a debtor’s debtor; or one father gave the other his claim in the presence of all three. This last needs examination, since the Rabbis may not have instituted “the presence of all three” where the claim cannot be collected in court, just as they did not for a ketuba (see Bava Kamma 89a). Finally: perhaps when both fathers are present and tell the priest to pay, he must return the money, and the authorization was needed only so that one father could recover it alone. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a2.2: But where he did not deny it we write: As for our practice nowadays of writing an authorization even where he denied it, Rabbeinu Tam says that the Nehardeans’ reason for not writing one is that it looks like a lie, as we say in Merubba (Bava Kamma 70a); and in Ketubot (85a) it is evident that we are not concerned about “looking like a lie.” I have discussed this at length in Merubba [ibid., s.v. amitaltelin].
tosafot:a5.1: If his son died within thirty days … he must return the five sela: The Kuntres [Rashi] explains: because he is a nefel. He explained so needlessly, for even if we know that his months were completed, the Merciful One made it depend on [his being] a month old.
tosafot:a5.2: After thirty, even though he did not give, he must give: At the end of Pesaḥim (121b) we say that the father of the son recites two blessings. And there is room for doubt: since [the son] has died, does he recite “Who has kept us alive” [sheheḥeyanu], given that he merits to fulfill the mitzva? And one should not wonder why we do not recite sheheḥeyanu on every circumcision as on every redemption of the son, for the mitzva of redemption of the son is different, since it is uncommon.
tosafot:a5.3: In brief: [On the thirtieth day and Rabbi Akiva.] At the start of HaḤoletz (Yevamot 36b) Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that whatever has lived thirty days among humans is not a nefel, so short of that it is a doubt; and it was stated there: if [the child] died within thirty days and [the widow] was betrothed, if she is an Israelite’s wife she performs ḥalitza. At the end of Rabbi Eliezer DeMila (Shabbat 136a) most texts read “died on the thirtieth day,” and so the Ri reads. Rabbeinu Ḥananel apparently reads “within thirty”: since the Rabbis here hold the thirtieth day is like the day before and Rabbi Akiva holds it doubtful, if the Rabbis and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagreed even about the thirtieth day, what difference would there be between the thirtieth day and within thirty? The She’iltot also read “within thirty.” But Halakhot Gedolot write that on the thirtieth day, even one who yawned and died is not a nefel according to the Rabbis, and only within thirty does Shabbat say that if he yawned and died all agree he was a nefel. That implies the reading “on the thirtieth day,” taking “died” plainly as yawned and died: one who lived that long and yawned and died on the thirtieth day is treated like one who fell from a roof within thirty. The reading can also be kept if it means one who fell from a roof or was eaten by a lion on the thirtieth day specifically, where we rely on the Rabbis, perhaps even for mourning, that he was already viable. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a5.4: Like the day before it: And if you say: at the start of HaḤoletz (Yevamot 37b) it seems we take it as obvious by Torah law that even within thirty he is alive, for it says: if he died within thirty and [his widow] was betrothed, if she is a priest’s wife she does not perform ḥalitza. One may answer that there it refers to one who fell from a roof or was eaten by a lion, according to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel at the end of Rabbi Eliezer DeMila; but here it refers to one who yawned and died, where all agree he was a nefel. And even if it refers here to one who fell from a roof, as there, there is no difficulty, for we likewise rule at the end of Im Lo Hevi (Shabbat 136a) like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, to be lenient regarding mourning, even though for a priest’s wife, where there is no other way, we rely on the Rabbis and permit her without ḥalitza. And if you say: here we are so lenient regarding mourning even for one we treat as certainly viable where there is no other way, as with the priest’s wife; yet in tractate Semaḥot, chapter 4 (halakha 2), it is taught that for doubtful cases one acts as an onen and mourns. One may answer that there it refers to a doubt whether he is a nine-month child of the first [husband] or a seven-month child of the later one, for it would be disgraceful that neither this one nor that one mourn, and he is certainly the son of one of them.
tosafot:b8.1: In brief: [On “For his own he goes and seizes from liened property, and with these five unencumbered ones he redeems his son.”] Tosafot ask: how can the priest seize liened property, when one does not collect from liened property where there is unencumbered property, and here there are five unencumbered? Had he redeemed his son first, it would be fine. And further: let the buyers then come back and take the five with which the priest redeemed the son, since either way their lien came before the son’s birth, for had the birth come first, the priest could seize from the buyers for the son as for the father. They answer that the buyers here bought from his father, so they cannot turn to property he himself acquired; or that the buyers’ deed did not say “what I shall acquire” [de’akni], and he acquired these unencumbered five afterward. (Even where de’akni was written it is a question in Mi SheMet, Bava Batra 157a; without it, we hold later property is not liened.) They then ask: if the sold land came from his father, fine; but how can land he himself acquired be liened for his own redemption, when that obligation took effect only when he came of age, and later acquisitions are not liened to the priest without de’akni? It must therefore speak of land he inherited from his father. Yet even for Rabbi Yehuda the son’s redemption can sometimes come first, as where he had nothing from his father, bought the land after coming of age and sold it after his son’s birth: then for his son’s redemption he goes and seizes from liened property. Alternatively, later acquisitions are liened for redemption even without de’akni, since the obligation rests on him at every moment, and since it counts as a loan written in a document, it is as if the document were written after he acquired the land. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b10.1: The five sela of the son, etc.: The tanna did not need to teach the guilt offering of silver shekels or valuations [in this list], for with the guilt offering it is written explicitly “in the shekel of the Sanctuary,” and valuations too are obviously in the shekel of the Sanctuary, since it is written: “And all your valuations shall be according to the shekel of the Sanctuary” (Leviticus 27:25).
tosafot:b12.1: In brief: Rashi explains Rabbi Asi’s “maneh of Tyre” as the one current in Tyre, whose sela is four zuz, each zuz the weight of a gold coin of two and a half pshitin by iron weight. He seems to have had this as a tradition from his teachers, and it implies that a silver dinar weighs the same as a gold one, as he also explains on the Torah (Mishpatim, the thirty shekels) that the shekel weighs four gold coins, half an ounce by the true weight of Cologne. Rabbeinu Tam disagrees, since a gold dinar weighs as much as two silver ones, as explained below. Rashi also explains that Rabbi Ḥanina’s Syrian sela, eight to a dinar, refers to the ordinary dinar of the Talmud, an eighth of the Tyrian dinar, and that Rabbi Ḥanina is a Tanna who disagrees with the mishna. But then the five sela would be a trifle: eight of them worth an eighth of a Tyrian dinar, itself only two and a half pshitin, so that for Rabbi Ḥanina the five sela of the son would not be worth one pashut of our coinage. Further, Rashi takes the dinar as a provincial dinar, which the Mishna usually calls zuz and the Talmud pshiti (as in Ketubot 67a, “fifty zuz pshiti”), whereas everywhere an unqualified dinara is gold, sold for twenty-five zuz, as in Kiddushin (40a), where Elijah gave Rav Kahana a bundle of dinars, and Rabbi Ami found a ship of dinars, meaning gold dinars. It seems better to explain that none of them disagree, and all come to explain the measure of the mishna: “Tyrian maneh” means five sela from a maneh of sela, the sela of the son. [The text here names Rabbi Ami.] Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b12.2: Rabbi Ami says: An Arabian dinar: that is, an Arabian dinar is worth five sela of the son; not as the Kuntres [Rashi] explained, that the Tyrian sela is the Arabian dinar. He also wrote, “I found in a responsum of the Babylonian Geonim that seven of the dinars mentioned throughout the Talmud, the dinar being six silver ma’a, make ten of those of Arabia,” and his words contradict each other. Since the Arabian dinar is smaller even than the dinar of the Talmud, the Tyrian sela cannot be the Arabian dinar, for a sela holds four of the Tyrian dinars mentioned throughout the Talmud, as we say in Kiddushin and everywhere. Rather, [Rabbi Ami] speaks of gold dinars, and the Arabian one is smaller than the Tyrian gold dinar, for the Tyrian is sold for twenty-five silver [dinars] and the Arabian for twenty, as I explained: its measure is that of the five sela of the son.
tosafot:b12.3: Rabbi Ḥanina says: Istera sesuraya: so it is written in most texts, but the Kuntres [Rashi] reads susarita. It seems both are named for Syria, as in Bava Kamma (83a) the word sursi refers to Syria. It is a Syrian sela, eight of which are sold for a dinar, that is, for a Syrian gold dinar, which is larger than the Tyrian gold dinar mentioned throughout the Talmud, since the Syrian is not sold for twenty-five. And this Syrian dinar, worth eight [sela] of the son, is thirty-two silver dinars, since the sela is four dinars.
gershom:a2.1: Where he denied it: because it looks like a lie.
gershom:a3.1: Rav Huna teaches: he adds to our mishna, [to the case of] one [wife] who had given birth and one who had not, of two men, who gave birth, etc. He adds: two males and a female, the priest has nothing here, for the one whose wife had not given birth can say: Perhaps my wife bore a male and a female, and I do not know which came out first. [Rabbeinu Gershom sets Rav Huna’s addition in the case of one woman who had given birth and one who had not; Rashi sets it in the case of two who had not.]
gershom:a4.1: And our tanna [does not teach it]: because you do not find it with a man and his two wives, one who had given birth and one who had not, for whichever way you look at it he is liable for five sela, since two males were born. [So] he does not teach it.
gershom:a5.1: If the son died within thirty: it speaks of the firstborn of any woman.
gershom:a6.1: Like the day before it: and he is exempt.
gershom:a7.1: Just as there: of the wilderness “and upward” is written, meaning thirty and more. A month is twenty-nine and a half days, and “upward” is one day more, which makes thirty and a half days, that is, after thirty. Therefore if he died on the thirtieth day it is like the day before it, and he is exempt. [The last words of the note are garbled in the printed text.]
gershom:a8.1: And Rabbi Akiva is uncertain whether we derive it: since it was necessary to write “and upward” with regard to valuations, they are two verses that come as one.
gershom:a9.1: But for themselves they do teach: for the “month” of the wilderness, of which “and upward” is written, and “those to be redeemed, from a month old,” both speak of a human firstborn. And perhaps they do teach; that is why he is uncertain, and says: If he gave, he does not take it back, etc.
gershom:a10.1: That the thirtieth day is like the one after it, and he is permitted to launder his clothes and cut his hair. [Rabbeinu Gershom seems to read Rav Ashi’s ruling as concerning the thirty days of mourning, the thirtieth day counting as already past.]
gershom:a12.1: Until they tell him that he was [not] redeemed: whether a slave, a woman or a minor, they are believed.
gershom:a13.1: Just as with the betrothal of a woman: where he said to her, “Be betrothed to me after thirty [days],” she is betrothed, even though the money was used up beforehand.
gershom:b1.1: There, it is in his power to betroth her from now, even within thirty; therefore it is a betrothal, even though the money was used up.
gershom:b2.1: But if he did not die, his son is redeemed, even though he gave it to him beforehand.
gershom:b3.1: Until they tell him that he was redeemed: so if they told him that he was redeemed, even though it was within thirty, he is redeemed.
gershom:b4.1: Is not like one written in a document: so he does not collect from liened property, and there are only the five unencumbered.
gershom:b5.1: The maneh of Tyre: twenty-five shekels to the maneh of the Torah.
gershom:b6.1: Rabbi Ami says: An Arabian dinar: this too is a sela.
gershom:b7.1: Istera sursaya: a sela of that place; they are light, so that eight of them are given for a gold dinar. A gold dinar is five pshitin by iron weight, a silver dinar two and a half by iron weight. And the rule of a gold dinar in Torah sela: it is to be sold only for six silver sela, which are twenty-four silver dinars, which are twenty-four zuz. And when Rabbi Yoḥanan [50a] says twenty-five zuz, that [extra] zuz goes to tip the scale for the twenty-four zuz, if each were weighed by itself.
gershom:b8.1: Another version: sursaya, that is, it is like a broker [sarsur], with which all trade is done. [The note ends with an unclear abbreviation.]
